newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Yorks Water sets $235 mln buyback plan.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Yorks Water sets $235 mln buyback plan.

text.p: Drought-blighted British water utility Yorkshire Water Plc said on Thursday it planned a capital reorganisation to reduce its equity and return up to 10 percent of its market value to shareholders as cash.

The company plans to divide each ordinary share into two new ordinary shares plus two B shares. It would then offer to buy back these B shares at their nominal value of 36 pence each, for a maximum outlay of about 145 million pounds ($235 million).
Thereafter, it would consolidate the ordinary shares at a rate of nine new ones for every 10 existing shares.
The announcement lifted Yorkshire Water shares to their highest level in almost seven months and analysts said it was likely to herald other similar buybacks in the industry soon.

Yorkshire chairman Brandon Gough said the company, which in the past has suffered from bad publicity after record droughts revealed big shortcomings in its ability to secure and deliver water, had made big investments in securing water supply.

"The group now wishes to improve financial efficiency in a way which allows all shareholders to participate, and believes the proposed capital reorganisation is the most effective way of achieving this," he said.
The move will raise gearing at the company up to as much as 35 percent from the current 20 percent.

Yorkshire also said it intends to maintain growth in total cash dividend at a rate of six to eight percent annually after inflation until 2000, subject only to there being no adverse change in the industry's political and regulatory environment.
Britain's opposition Labour Party, seen in opinion polls as the likely winner in the next general elections due by May 22, has declared its intention to impose a windfall tax on privatised utilities.

Yorkshire, which emerged from the Conservative government's drive to privatise public services over the past decade, said the aim of the cash-for-shares aspect of the capital reduction is to try and reach as many shareholders as possible.

Finance director Brian Wilson told reporters that, after considering special dividends and conventional buybacks, it had opted for a consolidation because "we wanted to have a method that gave all of our shareholders a chance to participate".
SBC Warburg, on behalf of Yorkshire Water, will offer to buy the new B shares free of dealing expenses.
Under the plan, a shareholder with 100 ordinary shares who sold his new B shares would end up with 180 new ordinary shares and 72 pounds cash.
"We believe that many shareholders will choose to sell them and that is a process which will lead to more debt and less equity on the balance sheet," Wilson explained.

As well as giving the firm's estimated 40,000 small investors in its home region of Yorkshire, northern England, a fairer chance of getting cash back than under a conventional buyback (mainly aimed at institutions), it was also hoped to improve the marketability of all the shares, Wilson said.

Asked how he expected shareholders to react to the package, which has to be approved at an extraordinary meeting on February 26, Wilson said: "We're very confident that our shareholders will find it a very attractive option."
All holders will, however, be taxed on any cash raised by their B share sale which will be treated as a disposal gain.
The terms, while more complex than many had anticipated, were broadly better than expected, said utility analyst Nigel Hawkins at the London branch of Yamaichi International.
"It appears to be a sensibile deal and certainly innovative," he added.
By 0950 GMT Yorkshire shares were trading up 13-1/2 pence at 731 pence, just off an earlier high of 735 pence. ($1=.6175 Pound)
